nameStory: Garden lobelia gets its name from the botanist Matthias de l'Obel, a 16th-century Flemish physician who studied plants. The 'garden' part distinguishes it from its wild cousins like cardinal flower and great blue lobelia that grow naturally in New England's wetlands and meadows. This little charmer earned its place in countless flower boxes and hanging baskets across New England, even though it originally called southern Africa home.
description: Garden lobelia is a small, delicate flowering plant that typically grows 4-8 inches tall and spreads into a trailing carpet of tiny blooms. Its flowers are distinctively two-lipped and asymmetrical, usually bright blue, purple, white, or pink, creating dense clusters that seem to float above the foliage. The small, narrow leaves are arranged alternately along slender, often drooping stems. This tender annual creates a cloud-like effect in containers and garden borders, blooming continuously through the growing season until frost.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny two-lipped flowers with three lower petals forming a fan and two smaller upper petals, creating an asymmetrical face-like appearance. The blooms feel papery-thin and are typically bright blue, though white and pink varieties exist.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow, lance-shaped leaves about half an inch long that feel smooth and slightly succulent. They're arranged alternately along the stem and have a fresh, slightly bitter scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing and spreading with trailing stems that cascade over container edges or form dense mats. The stems feel soft and slightly brittle, breaking easily when handled roughly.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny capsules that split open to release dust-like seeds so small they look like pepper flakes. The capsules feel dry and papery when mature.

habitat: Garden lobelia is not native to New England and is rarely found growing wild here. You'll spot it in cultivated settings like flower boxes, hanging baskets, container gardens, and as edging in formal flower beds. It prefers cool, moist conditions and partial shade, especially during hot summer afternoons.

seasonality.spring: Planted outdoors after last frost, young plants show bright green foliage and begin producing their first small clusters of flowers by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with masses of tiny flowers covering the plant. May slow down during the hottest weeks but resumes heavy flowering as temperatures moderate.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming vigorously through early fall, often looking its best during cool September and October weather until killed by first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies completely with frost as it's a tender annual. Only dried brown stems and spent seed capsules remain if not cleaned up.

funFact: Garden lobelia's flowers are so perfectly designed for tiny pollinators that they're mainly visited by small bees and butterflies, but the plant has a secret weapon - it can actually self-pollinate by curling its male parts down to touch its female parts when pollinators are scarce, ensuring it always produces those pepper-flake sized seeds!
confusionNotes: Garden lobelia's tiny size and trailing habit make it unlikely to be confused with its wild New England relatives like cardinal flower or great blue lobelia, which are much taller wetland plants. The small blue flowers might remind you of forget-me-nots, but lobelia's distinctive two-lipped flower shape (versus forget-me-not's flat, round flowers) makes them easy to tell apart.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'garden lobelia,' this plant belongs to the bellflower family, not the mint or snapdragon families that many two-lipped flowers belong to. Like its wild relatives, garden lobelia contains alkaloids that make it toxic if eaten, so it's purely ornamental despite its delicate, edible-looking appearance.
compareHints: Garden lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its New England native relatives like cardinal flower and great blue lobelia, which are tall, upright wetland plants. While the wild lobelias have similar two-lipped flowers, they're much larger and more tubular, designed for hummingbirds and larger pollinators rather than the tiny bees that visit garden lobelia's petite blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cardinal flower stands out dramatically from its lobelia relatives—while great blue lobelia produces similar tubular flowers in blue, and Indian tobacco has tiny pale flowers, only cardinal flower blazes in brilliant red.
Unlike its showier relatives cardinal flower (bright red) and great blue lobelia (deep blue), Indian tobacco has much smaller, paler flowers.
Among New England's lobelias, great blue lobelia is easily distinguished by its brilliant blue color and robust size.
Unlike its showy red cousin cardinal flower or the tall blue spikes of great blue lobelia, water lobelia is the only member of the lobelia family that lives completely underwater.
Among New England's lobelias, pale-spiked lobelia is the wallflower of the family with its subtle white or pale blue flowers.
Kalm's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its showy relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue, much larger).

Unlike its native Lobelia relatives such as cardinal flower or great blue lobelia which grow as upright leafy stems with showy flower spikes, matted pratia is a tiny mat-forming groundcover with individual star-shaped flowers.
Nuttall's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its famous relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue and tall).
